title: Sebaceous Adenitis
desc: Cyclosporine, vitamin A, isotretinoin and essential fatty acids, plus the topical descaling and moisturising protocol (baby-oil soaks, sulfur/salicylic shampoos, phytosphingosine).

meds.name: Cyclosporine
meds.desc: suppresses the immune attack on the sebaceous glands
meds.note: 5 mg/kg once daily. Give on an empty stomach where tolerated. Response is slow — allow several months before judging it.

meds.name: Vitamin A
meds.note: 400 IU/kg once daily, to a MAXIMUM of 20,000 IU per day. The calculated figure above is not capped — for any dog over about 50 kg, dispense 20,000 IU rather than the calculated dose.

meds.name: Isotretinoin
meds.note: Held in reserve on this sheet: potentially problematic side effects and high expense.

meds.name: Omega-3 fatty acids
meds.note: Consider changing the food to Hill's j/d Mobility instead — it contains 2% DHA & EPA, about the highest available, and is probably more effective than a regular diet plus Welactin.

meds.name: Dermoscent Essential 6 Spot-On
meds.doseText: one spot-on application to the base of the neck
meds.note: Available over the counter. Applied to the base of the neck / between the shoulder blades in the same way as a flea and tick preventive.

meds.name: Douxo S3 SEB shampoo
meds.doseText: a bath with Douxo S3 SEB shampoo

meds.name: Sulfur & salicylic acid shampoo
meds.doseText: a medicated bath, 10 minutes contact time
meds.note: Scale can also be lifted with soft brushing.

meds.name: Baby oil soak
meds.doseText: a 50:50 baby oil and water soak over the whole coat
meds.note: Leave on as long as possible — 30 to 60 minutes is ideal, up to an hour — then degrease in a Dawn dish-soap bath and moisturise afterwards.

meds.name: Propylene glycol
meds.doseText: a topical application of propylene glycol
freqs: daily at first, then 2–3 times weekly

meds.name: Phytosphingosine spray
meds.doseText: a topical application of phytosphingosine spray

meds.name: Hydrating spray
meds.desc: keeps the coat and skin moisturised
meds.doseText: a topical application of hydrating spray

notes.Shape of the plan: Systemic therapy (cyclosporine ± vitamin A) to stop the glandular destruction, essential fatty acids to support the skin, and a topical routine to lift scale and re-moisturise. The topical work matters as much as the tablets.
notes.Conditioning: Conditioning shampoos and sprays after every descaling bath — the aim is to remove scale without stripping the coat.
notes.Expectations: This is a lifelong management problem, not a cure. Response is slow, and the topical routine is what most owners notice the biggest difference from.

dischargeBlocks.title: What this condition is
dischargeBlocks.text:
Sebaceous adenitis is a condition where {name}'s own immune system attacks the small oil glands in the skin. Without those glands the skin becomes dry and scaly and the coat thins.

It is managed rather than cured. With a steady routine most dogs do well, but it takes months to see the full benefit — please do not judge the plan too early.

dischargeBlocks.title: The bathing routine
dischargeBlocks.text:
This is the part that makes the most visible difference, and it is the part that takes your time.

- Use the medicated shampoo we dispensed, and leave it on for a full 10 minutes before rinsing. Set a timer — this is the step most often cut short.
- Soft brushing before the bath helps lift the loose scale.
- Follow every medicated bath with the conditioner or moisturising spray.
- For heavy scale we may ask you to do an oil soak: half baby oil, half warm water, worked right through the coat, left on for 30 to 60 minutes, then washed out with Dawn dish soap and followed by a moisturiser. It is messy — do it somewhere you do not mind.

dischargeBlocks.title: About the medication
dischargeBlocks.text:
Give every dose as directed and do not stop when the coat starts to look better — the improvement depends on staying on it.

Call us before stopping or changing anything.

dischargeBlocks.title: Follow up
dischargeBlocks.text: Please book a recheck as we discussed so we can see how the skin and coat are responding, and call us sooner if {name} becomes itchy, develops sores or a smell, or seems unwell on the medication.
